# Sterilising instruments and dressings by heat (`heat_sterilisation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, spontaneous_generation_refuted, safety_valve_boiler, antiseptics
- Core idea: Cleaning removes blood and debris that shield microbes. Boiling reduces infection risk but can leave bacterial spores alive. Sterilising surgical instruments requires a validated process. Saturated steam must contact every surface after air is removed; a gravity-displacement steriliser typically exposes wrapped instruments to 121 °C for 30 minutes once the load reaches temperature. The required cycle depends on the load and the equipment. Check cycle indicators, dry the packs and protect them from contamination until use. Repeated boiling is unreliable for instruments.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sterilising the knife and then laying it on the table, wiping it on an apron or handling it with unwashed fingers
  - Dipping instruments in hot water for a moment
  - Boiling without first cleaning off dried blood and pus
  - Assuming boiling kills everything; spores survive, which is why Tyndall and Pasteur's opponents got growth in boiled hay broth
  - A sealed pressure vessel without a safety valve
- History: europe: 1760s – Spallanzani shows long boiling in sealed flasks prevents growth; 1810 Appert preserves food by heat; 1877 Tyndall finds heat-resistant spores; 1879 Chamberland's autoclave; 1881 Koch, Gaffky and Loeffler show steam beats dry heat and chemicals; 1886 von Bergmann introduces steam-sterilised dressings; 1891–1892 Schimmelbusch's system of asepsis; americas: c. 1890 – Halsted introduces rubber gloves at Johns Hopkins
- Read:
  - Robert Koch, Georg Gaffky and Friedrich Loeffler, Versuche über die Verwerthbarkeit heisser Wasserdämpfe zu Desinfectionszwecken, Mittheilungen aus dem Kaiserlichen Gesundheitsamte (1881)
  - Curt Schimmelbusch, Anleitung zur aseptischen Wundbehandlung (1892)
  - Thomas Schlich, Asepsis and bacteriology: a realignment of surgery and laboratory science, Medical History (2012)
